This was an internal assessment in the same chat and model, using the same parent premises. [Claim assessment](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/reviews/14_TND_OC_E12_R1_FULL_MARKED_PAIR_CLAIM_ASSESSMENT_20261108.md)

[Continuation and model guidance](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/continuation-notes/20_TND_OC_AFTER_E12_FULL_PAIR_ASSESSMENT_AND_MODEL_CHANGE_20261108.md)

I updated the research register, refreshed OC chat0008, and queued capture of this final reply.
What is the current status of the results? Can you explain it at a high level?
I’ll check the OC register and assessment so I can separate what’s proved from what still needs to be measured.

**The OC branch has proved a bound on how fast the smoothed zero correlations can change. The correlations themselves still need to be computed.**

Think of each zero as a small Gaussian spot on the complex plane. E10 tracks the resulting density of individual zeros, the density of ordered pairs of distinct zeros, and the connected pair density, which subtracts the product of the two average individual densities. For each fixed height range and blur width in the study, E10 proves that the largest change anywhere in each profile is bounded by a constant times the elapsed Newman time. The bound holds from \(0\) to \(1/2\), including when zeros coincide, and needs no lower bound on the gap between them. [E10 proof note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/notes/17_TND_OC_E10_R1_FULL_MARKED_PAIR_EVOLUTION_PROOF_20261108.md)

**E12 accepted all six claims unchanged** in an internal review using the same model and inherited premises. The key limitation is that the bound controls the *amount* of change. The quadratic example shows that a collision can satisfy the bound and still produce a kink. Collision exclusion therefore remains a separate question. [E12 assessment](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/reviews/14_TND_OC_E12_R1_FULL_MARKED_PAIR_CLAIM_ASSESSMENT_20261108.md)

If the next objective is to see what the actual profile looks like, **E09 is ready and unstarted**. It targets a certified time-zero benchmark at \(T=1000\). A successful uniform approximation would give E10 a starting profile to carry forward with a controlled error. [Continuation note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/continuation-notes/20_TND_OC_AFTER_E12_FULL_PAIR_ASSESSMENT_AND_MODEL_CHANGE_20261108.md)
Can you explain in more depth how the relevant statistical measures are defined. I'm still not sure it aligns with what I'm thinking. I was thinking more like a locally averaged pair density.
I’ll compare the definitions in the proof with a density built by averaging pairs near a given height. The distinction is which pair coordinates the statistic keeps.
Sorry - locally averaged distance metric, closer to a Vandermonde determinant
That points to a different observable. I’ll check how the project’s earlier Vandermonde formulation relates to an average of distances between nearby zeros.

The closest match is a **local geometric mean of pair distances**. Put a window around a height \(X\), take the distances between the zeros in that window, and combine them multiplicatively. That gives one number per window. Slide the window to see how that number varies with height.

For \(N\ge2\) zeros in a window, write \(d_{jk}=|z_j-z_k|/\ell\), where \(\ell\) is a reference spacing. Then the statistic is
\[
D_X=\left(\prod_{j<k}d_{jk}\right)^{1/\binom N2}.
\]
The product inside the parentheses is exactly the **magnitude of the Vandermonde determinant** in the rescaled zero coordinates. The exponent puts the result on a per-pair scale. You can make the window smooth by giving each zero a weight \(w_j\) and taking a weighted average of \(\log d_{jk}\) with weights \(w_jw_k\), then exponentiating. Both versions use the full complex distance. A conjugate pair \(x\pm iy\) has distance \(2|y|\) even though both zeros have the same real coordinate. [Original OC formulation](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/research-overview/01_TND_OC_RESEARCH_OVERVIEW_20261107.md)

The geometric mean is sensitive to a close pair in a way the ordinary mean isn’t. For three points at \(0,\delta,1\), the mean distance stays at \(2/3\) as \(\delta\to0\), while the geometric mean \([\delta(1-\delta)]^{1/3}\) goes to zero. An exact collision makes the Vandermonde product zero.

**This is where it differs from E10.** E10 keeps a whole map of where pairs occur, blurs each zero’s position, and averages the maps over window centers. Your distance statistic would first combine the pair distances **inside each window**, and then, if desired, average those local scores over nearby centers. The underlying pair measure can express the log-distance average, but E10’s bound at fixed Gaussian blur does not control the singular \(\log d\) at a collision. A version with a distance floor would be a separate, regularized observable. [E10 proof](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/notes/17_TND_OC_E10_R1_FULL_MARKED_PAIR_EVOLUTION_PROOF_20261108.md)

I'm not sure if that is the best though. I think the VDW determinant appears in the joint probability density for the zeros, which is one of the reasons we were also looking at marginals. Does that resonate more with the recent work?
Yes, that distinction matters. I’ll check how the recent work defines its joint law and marginals, and where a Vandermonde factor would enter.

Yes. **The Vandermonde as a factor in a joint density is closer to the recent work.** I took your earlier reference to it as a suggestion to measure the determinant on each local configuration. Your clarification puts the emphasis on the **two-zero marginal of a joint law**, which is the object OC has been developing.

In a random-matrix model, the joint density of all \(N\) points can take the form
\[
p_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\propto
\underbrace{\prod_{j<k}|x_j-x_k|^2}_{|\Delta(x)|^2}
\prod_j w_0(x_j).
\]
The Vandermonde factor weights entire configurations. To find the pair density at \(u,v\), hold two coordinates there and integrate over all the others. The result reflects how those two points interact with the rest of the configuration as well as with each other. [Model calculation and original OC formulation](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/research-overview/01_TND_OC_RESEARCH_OVERVIEW_20261107.md#2-what-vandermonde-marginalization-does)

**OC constructs the corresponding marginal from the actual zeros.** In a finite window, take the observed zero configuration, randomly order its labels, and blur each position slightly. That defines an empirical joint law. Its two-coordinate marginal is the sum over distinct pairs, divided by \(N(N-1)\) for an unweighted window. The recent work uses the weighted pair-count version, averages over a shared window center, and keeps both complex coordinates. E10 proves how fast that pair density can change with Newman time. [Marginal construction](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/notes/09_TND_OC_FULL_GAUSSIAN_MARGINALS_AND_CANONICAL_TRANSFER_20261108.md#2-the-primary-hierarchy-and-the-full-joint-law) · [E10 proof](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/notes/17_TND_OC_E10_R1_FULL_MARKED_PAIR_EVOLUTION_PROOF_20261108.md)

So the recent work gives you **the empirical side of the comparison**. The open question is whether a Vandermonde-based model predicts that local pair marginal, with a justified error. Even agreement at the pair level would leave the full joint law open.
Can you explain how this is localized in height? Is this related to the weighting?
I’ll check the exact window in E10 and distinguish its height weighting from the Gaussian blur and the average over centers.

Yes. **The window weights are what localize the pair density in height.** Pick a center \(X\), give each zero a weight based on how far its height is from \(X\), and give each pair the product of its two weights. Both zeros have to be near the **same** center to contribute.

In E10, \(x_j=\Re z_j\) is the height coordinate. The window gives a zero full weight when \(|x_j-X|\le 1/2\), tapers smoothly to zero between \(1/2\) and \(1\), and gives it zero weight at distance \(1\) or more. For example, a zero in the middle paired with one whose edge weight is \(0.4\) contributes with weight \(0.4\). At Newman time zero, \(x_j=2\gamma_j\), so a distance of \(1\) in this coordinate is half a unit in ordinary zeta height. [Exact window definition](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/manuscript/sections/12_full_pair_transfer.tex)

The procedure is to **weight locally, recenter, then average**. At each \(X\), move the origin to \(X\) and apply a small Gaussian blur to make the pair map smooth. Then slide \(X\) uniformly over \([T,2T]\) and average those maps. The final result describes what pairs look like *within a local window*, averaged over a broad range of heights. Keeping the map at each \(X\) would let you see how the local picture changes with height. [E10 definitions](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/notes/17_TND_OC_E10_R1_FULL_MARKED_PAIR_EVOLUTION_PROOF_20261108.md#setting-and-theorem)

In the Vandermonde picture, the weight \(w_0\) helps define the model’s **joint law**. The sliding window weight plays the role of an **observation rule**. It selects which pairs you count from the zeros or from a model. You could apply the same observation rule to both and compare their local pair densities.
Why not weight with a Gaussian? That might be easier to control analytically for more explicit calculations using the actual theta source?
I’ll check what the compact window buys in the current proof and what a Gaussian window would simplify in a calculation from the theta source.

Yes. **A Gaussian is a natural choice for the height window**, especially if the aim is to get a more explicit formula for a locally averaged pair density. The compact window in E10 had a practical advantage: at each center it selects finitely many zero labels, so the proof can handle all relevant collisions in a bounded box. A Gaussian gives every zero some weight. The existing zero-count bounds make the resulting tails summable, but a Gaussian version of the proof would need to account for them. [E10 proof](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/notes/17_TND_OC_E10_R1_FULL_MARKED_PAIR_EVOLUTION_PROOF_20261108.md) · [Gaussian window and tails](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/notes/09_TND_OC_FULL_GAUSSIAN_MARGINALS_AND_CANONICAL_TRANSFER_20261108.md)

A Gaussian gives you a clean split between **where a pair is** and **how far apart its members are**. If the height weight is \(w_X(x)=e^{-(x-X)^2/(2h^2)}\), and the pair has midpoint \(m=(x_j+x_k)/2\) and height difference \(d=x_j-x_k\), then
\[
w_X(x_j)w_X(x_k)=e^{-(m-X)^2/h^2}\,e^{-d^2/(4h^2)}.
\]
The first factor localizes the pair near \(X\). The second gives more weight to smaller height differences. This separates the two roles exactly, while leaving the imaginary coordinates available as marks.

There’s also an exact simplification on the **theta source** side. If you convolve \(H_\lambda\) itself in the horizontal direction with a normalized Gaussian of width \(h\), each cosine mode of frequency \(t\) picks up the factor \(e^{-h^2t^2/2}\). That changes \(H_\lambda\) into \(H_{\lambda-h^2/2}\). The weighted **zero** density, however, comes from the Laplacian of \(\log|H_\lambda|\). The Gaussian convolution identity for \(H_\lambda\) does not pass through that logarithm. For the pair density, the outstanding calculation is still a joint average of two log fields at the same center. [Theta-to-pair formula](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/notes/14_TND_OC_B08_ARITHMETIC_MARGINAL_COLLISION_FRICTION_20261108.md)

So your suggestion buys something concrete: a simpler kernel in midpoint and separation coordinates. The question to test is whether that simpler kernel also lets us bound the **joint logarithmic average** more sharply from the actual theta source.

Excellent, can you modify the research overview, plan and progress file to include this, and also write a note elaborating on your findings, and then write a continuation note with a recommended model to continue working on the idea?

I’ll add the Gaussian height window as a distinct OC research direction. I’ll document the identities we already have, the estimates still needed for the actual theta source, and a bounded next task with a model recommendation.

The note now has a concrete extension: the Gaussian window gives an exact formula for averaging each pair over centers. The inherited zero counts and safe-line bound also justify removing the compact cutoff on both the zero and log-source sides. The next task can focus on whether those formulas yield a useful estimate for the joint theta term.

I updated the OC [research overview](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/research-overview/02_TND_OC_MARGINAL_PRIORITIES_RESEARCH_OVERVIEW_20261108.md), [plan](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/research-plan/02_TND_OC_MARGINAL_PRIORITIES_RESEARCH_PLAN_20261108.md), and [progress register](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/research-progress/02_TND_OC_MARGINAL_PRIORITIES_RESEARCH_PROGRESS_20261108.md) to add Gaussian height localization as **TND-OC-B10 r1**.

The [research note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/notes/18_TND_OC_GAUSSIAN_HEIGHT_WINDOW_AND_THETA_SOURCE_20261109.md) derives an exact formula for averaging each pair over window centers and bounds the tails from distant zeros and the log-source integral. The remaining question is whether those simpler formulas yield a useful estimate for the joint theta term.

**Next: B10 r1 with GPT-6 Astra.** The [continuation note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/08_theta_observables_newman_dynamics/03_operator_imaginary_time_evolution/02_localized_zero_correlations/continuation-notes/21_TND_OC_GAUSSIAN_HEIGHT_WINDOW_AND_MODEL_CHANGE_20261109.md) includes a pasteable prompt to compare the full marked pair with one separation projection that retains both imaginary marks. Astra is recommended because the next step is to choose and justify a proof route. B10 is ready and unstarted. [OpenAI model guidance](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/model-selection)
